title: ChaosNexus: A Foundation Model for ODE-based Chaotic System Forecasting with Hierarchical Multi-scale Awareness
claim: Chaotic systems have much broader, higher spectral entropy than general time series, so models must handle richer spectral structure.
layout: 3 panels: wide histogram on top, two spectra below; overlaid KDE curves
description: A three-panel figure of plots. Panel (a), spanning the top, is an overlaid histogram with smoothed density curves of normalized spectral entropy (x-axis 0 to 1, y-axis probability). General time series, in orange, form a sharp peak near 0.07. Chaotic systems, in teal, form a broad, flat distribution spread from about 0.0 to 0.8. Panels (b) and (c) sit side by side underneath. They show noisy dark-blue power spectra for Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96, with power on the y-axis and frequency (1/t) from 0 to 3 on the x-axis. Lorenz-63 power decays with frequency. Lorenz-96 power stays broadband and high out to high frequencies. The eye goes first to the tall orange peak against the broad teal distribution.
caption: Motivating observations. (a) Spectral entropy distributions of synthetic chaotic systems [ref] versus general time series [ref] (including Electricity, ETT, and Exchange Rate). (b--c) Power spectra of representatives from Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems.
abstract: Foundation models have shown great promise in achieving zero-shot or few-shot forecasting for ODE-based chaotic systems via large-scale pretraining. However, existing architectures often fail to capture the multi-scale temporal structures and distinct spectral characteristics of chaotic dynamics. To address this, we introduce ChaosNexus, a foundation model for chaotic system forecasting underpinned by the proposed ScaleFormer architecture. By processing temporal contexts across hierarchically varying patch sizes, ChaosNexus effectively captures long-range dependencies and preserves high-frequency fluctuations. To address heterogeneity across distinct systems, we integrate Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers into each ScaleFormer block and explicitly condition the final forecasts on a learned frequency fingerprint, providing the model with a global spectral view of the system. Extensive evaluations on over 9,000 synthetic systems demonstrate that ChaosNexus achieves superior fidelity in long-term attractor statistics while maintaining competitive point-wise accuracy. Furthermore, in real-world applications, it achieves a remarkable zero-shot mean error below 1Â°C for 5-day station-based weather forecasting. Codes are available at https://github.com/TomXaxaxa/ChaosNexus.
